"Wishing to cause sentient beings to attain [this state], he manifested this auspicious sign."
The commentary says:
This explains its meaning. What is the intention behind the emission of light?
It is because they desire to cause others to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult to believe.
Previously, two truths were taught; now, one reality is discussed. This causes them to abandon the former ultimate and adopt the present new ultimate; therefore, it is called "difficult to believe."
Not only is faith difficult, but the essential meaning is also difficult.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "O sons of good family" up to "throughout incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*"),
the commentary says:
Below are eight causes, which are collectively divided into two sections:
first, the prose (long passage), and second, the verse (gāthā).
The prose section is further divided into two parts:
The first seven [sections] provide answers by citing specific matters, while the final one provides an answer by showing the identity between the ancient and the present.
The initial text is divided into three parts:
the first is an answer that praises its rarity; the second is an answer that reveals subsequent excellence; and the last five are answers that detail shared activities.
The first section is the response praising what is rare. The title of this treatise is *Manifesting the Rare Causes*, because [the causes] cannot be obtained within a limited time.

Within this, there are four parts: first, praising the rarity of the long duration of time; second, praising the rarity of the Buddha’s name; third, praising the rarity of the excellence of the Dharma; and fourth, praising the rarity of the response regarding the benefits for those born [in that realm].
This is the first point.
The Treatise states:
"That which is inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable is shown because it cannot be found even after passing through incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
The Sanskrit term is *asaṃkhyeya*, which is erroneously transliterated as *asaṃkhyi*; it means "incalculable.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"The fifty-second number, accumulated from one up to ten, reaches its limit at this count and is called *asaṃkhyeya*. Originally there were sixty numbers, but eight have been lost through transmission."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* enumerates one hundred and twenty items; this is the one hundred and twelfth.
"Kalpa" (劫) is abbreviated as "jie" (劫), which here means "differentiation" (分別); it carries the sense of the differentiation of temporal divisions.
"Inconceivable" means it transcends the realm of emotional conceptualization.
"Incomparable" means it transcends the realm of verbal discourse.
"Immeasurable" means it is not within the realm of analogy or calculation.
In this sutra, "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) refers to that which transcends the categories of calculation and analogy;
"boundless" (*ananta*) refers to that which transcends the category of time;
and "inconceivable" (*acintya*) refers to that which transcends the category of intellectual deliberation.
This is equivalent to exceeding four parts of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The "Bodhisattvabhūmi" states that there are two kinds of kalpas:
first, those measured by days, nights, and years; second, asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states:
"Some say that one increase and one decrease constitute one kalpa—namely, those of famine, pestilence, and warfare;
others say that twenty kalpas constitute one kalpa—namely, that of the Brahmakāyika devas."
Alternatively, forty [of these] constitute one kalpa, referring to the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā;
alternatively, sixty of these constitute one kalpa, referring to Mahābrahmā;
alternatively, eighty of these constitute one kalpa, referring to the kalpa of the fire disaster; for the Heaven of Limited Light, this lifespan is calculated as two such kalpas.
Alternatively, seven fire calamities constitute one water calamity kalpa, referring to the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
or eight cycles of seven fire calamities and one cycle of seven water calamities constitute one wind calamity kalpa, referring to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Counting these up to the point where they can no longer be counted constitutes one *asaṃkhyeya*.

It is only after cultivating the causes for three such great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas that one attains Buddhahood; furthermore, there are ten distinct categories of kalpas, including the Bhadrakalpa and others.

According to the text of the ancient *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the stages prior to the [first] ground are divided into three, and each of the ten grounds is likewise divided into three, totaling thirty-three asaṃkhyeya kalpas. Among these, those prior to the seventh ground are considered "small," those from the eighth, ninth, and tenth grounds are "middling," and those prior to the [first] ground are "great."

Although there are such differences in the measurement of kalpas, according to this treatise, the various kalpas spoken of in a single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* primarily rely on five types:
first, night; second, day; third, month; fourth, season; and fifth, year.

Now, this is based on immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* eons, and not other great eons (*mahākalpa*), because it is intended to reveal that the Buddhas appear only once in the course of countless great eons, and because what Mañjuśrī perceives extends to an extreme distance.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, there was a Buddha... up to 'the Buddha, the World-Honored One'.
The commentary states:
This praises the rarity of the Buddha's name and title.
“Sūryacandrapradīpa” is a specific name, while “Tathāgata” and those that follow are general names.
The sun possesses two capacities:
first, it guides through illumination; second, it brings things to completion.
The moon has two capacities:
first, it removes heat; second, it provides coolness.
A lamp has two capacities:
First, it destroys darkness; second, it transmits illumination.

This reveals that the Buddha can lead the deluded to awakening, perfecting their capacity as vessels and ripening their faculties, removing the heat of afflictions and attaining the coolness of nirvana. It eternally shatters ignorance, transforming beings and transmitting the Dharma; thus, it expresses the distinct name "Rare" (Āścarya).
According to the explanation of the ten titles in the eighty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they are:

first, Tathāgata; second, Arhat; third, Samyaksaṃbuddha; fourth, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; fifth, Sugata; sixth, Lokavid; seventh, Anuttara-puruṣa-damya-sārathi; eighth, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām; ninth, Buddha; and tenth, Bhagavat.
"Tathāgata" is the initial general introduction; it serves as the general introduction for the nine subsequent titles.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Because he has come to Bodhi through the sūtras and dharmas taught by the Buddhas of the past—the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eleven kinds of emptiness, and so forth—he is called Tathāgata."

Furthermore, the present Śākyamuni, like all past Buddhas, relied upon the various teachings to cultivate practices such as the six perfections and contemplated principles such as the eleven kinds of emptiness, thereby attaining the fruit of Bodhi; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata, which refers to the Sambhogakāya Buddha.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This refers to the Dharmakāya Buddha.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Because one comes by means of the path of reality as it is and attains perfect enlightenment, one is called a Tathāgata.
Although this meaning is roughly correct, it is not the tenet of this school.
The treatise states:
"An 'Arhat' (Saṃyaksaṃbuddha) refers to one who is eternally liberated from all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the term "Arhat," this is correctly translated as "one who is worthy" (*arhat*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"He should have already eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he should be free from birth in discrete segments, and he should receive sublime offerings.

As explained previously in the root treatise regarding the interpretation of the sūtras, there are fifteen meanings; however, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and this very sūtra take only the destruction of the thieves of the afflictions as the definition of an Arhat, while the permanent severance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is termed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Arhatship is a common virtue; that which is below Perfect Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi) is an uncommon virtue.

The older translation uses "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), which refers to Perfect Enlightenment, Equal Enlightenment, and Perfect Equal Enlightenment, respectively excluding the three types of outsiders, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, and Bodhisattvas.
One who is perfected in knowledge and conduct is one who possesses the bases of knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*). "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*):
first, the knowledge of recollecting past abodes; second, the knowledge of death and rebirth; and third, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
"Practice" refers to the practice of restraint and the practice of cultivation.
The practice of cultivation refers to the pure manifestation of the three types of action and right livelihood.

Furthermore, the four kinds of dharma of the higher mind that constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life are the practice of abiding; these two are subsumed under the practice of cultivation.
Guarding the sense faculties is the practice of restraint.

When these two practices and the three types of supernormal knowledge are all perfected, the Tathāgata thereby manifests the three ways in which he need not guard himself and the quality of non-forgetfulness; by not committing transgressions, he attains mundane meditative concentration and thus restrains self-inflicted asceticism.

In this context, "not committing transgressions" refers to the purity of the three types of action; that is, through the three forms of non-protection and the guarding of the sense faculties, one attains the state of being free from forgetfulness, mundane meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and dwelling in happiness in the present life, thereby precluding self-mortification.
Therefore, it is said that his knowledge and conduct are perfected.
As for "Sugata" (Well-Gone), it refers to one who, throughout the long night, has been endowed with all aspects of the two qualities of self-benefit and benefit for others.
"Gata" means "gone."
This means that having attained *bodhi*, one proceeds through the long night of birth and death, possessing all kinds of meritorious deeds and virtuous qualities that benefit both oneself and others;
therefore, he is called the "Well-Gone" (*sugata*).

He is the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*) because he has thoroughly mastered both the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel (the environment). By virtue of his wisdom regarding the past and future limits of the world of sentient beings—namely, the knowledge of former abodes and the cycle of birth and death—he understands the differences in the mental activities of beings across the three periods of time due to the eighty-four thousand variations in their conduct at all times. Furthermore, he thoroughly understands the world of the vessel and so forth, as he clearly knows the infinite processes of formation and destruction in the ten directions, such as the eastern quarter.

Furthermore, because one thoroughly understands the intrinsic nature, causes and conditions, gratification, disadvantages, renunciation, and the path leading to transcendence regarding all phenomena in the world—namely, knowing the fruit of their intrinsic nature.
"Causes and conditions" refers to the cause; this is the general statement, while the remaining four truths are to be applied accordingly.

Regarding the "Unsurpassed Great Man, the Tamer of Men": formerly it was translated as "Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men. Because his wisdom is peerless and nothing surpasses it, he is called "Unsurpassed.
Within the present life, the Buddha’s body is endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, and thus he is a "Great Man."
Furthermore, because he is preeminent among those who discipline immeasurable men and is supremely exalted, he is explained by this subsequent [epithet].
What was formerly called "Unsurpassed Being, Tamer of Men" [is thus further clarified].

The Teacher of Gods and Humans (Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām) is so called because those gods and humans possess the power and capacity to understand the most profound meanings and diligently cultivate correct practice; other realms of existence lack these qualities and therefore are not designated as "teachers."

Regarding the term "Buddha," it refers to one who has ultimately severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and has manifested equal and perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) by attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; that is, one who possesses the two types of wisdom and awakens both oneself and others.

"Bhagavān" was formerly translated as "World-Honored One. He sits serenely and peacefully upon the sublime seat of bodhi, effortlessly destroying all demonic armies; by virtue of his great power, he immediately shatters the four māras.
As stated in a verse from the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:
"Sovereignty, brilliance, and physical excellence, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility—know that the possession of these six meanings is collectively termed 'Bhagavat'."

"Bhagavat" is a sound; in the Sanskrit language, it means "possessing virtue. If one possesses this title of Bhagavat, they are naturally able to destroy the four māras and must necessarily possess six virtues:
first, the sense of mastery, because they are forever unbound by any afflictions;
second, the sense of blazing intensity, because they have been refined and tempered by the fiercely burning fire of wisdom.
Third is the meaning of majesty, because he is adorned with the thirty-two marks and so forth;
fourth is the meaning of renown, because there is no one who does not know the Buddha’s supreme name;
fifth is the meaning of auspiciousness, because he constantly gives rise to skillful means to benefit sentient beings.
The sixth meaning is "nobility," because he is revered by both the mundane and supramundane worlds;
thus he is now called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavat*), while the preceding five meanings are absent [in this specific context].
The Sūtra states: "He expounds the True Dharma up to the characteristics of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
The commentary states:
The following praises the Dharma as supreme, wondrous, and rare.
As it says in [Sutra] 83:
"It possesses ten virtues.
First is excellence in the beginning, meaning that at the time of hearing it, joy arises.
Second is excellence in the middle, meaning that at the time of practice, there is no hardship, as one remains far removed from the two extremes and proceeds by way of the Middle Way."
"Third, it is 'good in the end,' meaning that it is ultimately free from all defilements, and because its final limit is the ultimate transcendence of all desire.

Because the *dharmatā* is free from defilement, those who are able to train in it are likewise free from defilement; through the culmination of practice, they attain the fruit that is free from defilement.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Praising generosity is called the 'goodness at the beginning'; praising the observance of precepts is called the 'goodness in the middle'; and praising the two fruits of rebirth in the heavens or pure lands is called the 'goodness at the end.'"
Furthermore, it is said that Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna are also called the "three excellences.
The *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states:

"Knowing suffering and abandoning its origin is called 'excellent in the beginning'; practicing the right path is called 'excellent in the middle'; realizing cessation is called 'excellent in the end. These are the excellences of the beginning, middle, and end for the Śrāvakas; [the same applies to the others]."

The Sūtra says: "He shows all sentient beings the places of birth-and-death and karmic retribution."
The commentary states:
Of the nine and a half verses that follow, as currently seen, there are five sections:

the first half-verse concerns sentient beings of the six realms; three verses concern seeing the Buddha; one verse concerns hearing the Dharma; one verse concerns seeing the fourfold assembly; and four verses concern seeing the bodhisattvas. There is no verse concerning entering parinirvāṇa or the erection of stupas.
This is the first [point].
"Abode" (sthāna) refers to the destination of retribution, for it is the place where one returns due to the causes of karma.
Alternatively, "abode" refers to the principle (nyāya), for there exists this principle that virtuous causes produce virtuous fruits and non-virtuous causes produce non-virtuous fruits.
"Place" refers to a location; it is the location where one experiences the fruits of good and evil karma.
As the Sūtra says: "The reason for seeing all Buddha-lands is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light."
The commentary states:
The three verses below concerning the vision of the Buddha are divided into three parts:
first, the vision of the pure land; second, the vision of making offerings; and third, the actual vision of the Buddha.
This is the first point.

Regarding the fact that the light of Śākyamuni is entirely golden, while that of Candrasūryapradīpa is the color of lapis lazuli and crystal: it is because the Mahāyāna is pure, uniform, and worthy of veneration that [Śākyamuni’s light] is exclusively golden; it is because his manifold virtues are perfectly complete that [Candrasūryapradīpa’s light] is of various colors; and it is because they manifest through mutual reflection.
In Sanskrit it is called *vaiḍūrya*; abbreviated, it is called *liuli* (lapis lazuli). It possesses various colors.

*Sphaṭika* is translated as "crystal" (*shuijing*), also as "water-jade" (*shuiyu*), or as "white pearl" (*bai zhu*). It is erroneously transliterated as *poli*—where "li" is pronounced with the *lì-sī* (力私) tone.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Within the mountain caves, ice that has persisted for over a thousand years transforms into crystal (*sphaṭika*).
Since the lands of the West are hot and lack ice, what substance could possibly transform into it?
This is merely a type of stone found everywhere.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, “And seeing the various devas and humans, all of whom were upright, dignified, and exceedingly subtle,” the commentary says:
In these two verses, the first describes seeing the eight classes of beings making offerings, while the latter describes seeing the Buddha.
The sutra states: "As if within pure lapis lazuli... [until] expounding the profound meaning of the Dharma."
The commentary states:
This is the hearing of the Dharma.

The Buddha emits light that illuminates himself, or the assembly illuminates the Buddha; in this manner, it is seen from afar like a golden image appearing and preaching the Dharma within lapis lazuli.
The Sūtra states: "In each and every Buddha-field... until he sees all those great assemblies.
The Commentary says:
This refers to seeing the fourfold assembly.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, “There may be certain bhikṣus who come to hear the Dharma seeking the Buddha-way,” the commentary states:

These four verses show the various causes and conditions, faith-understandings (adhimukti), characteristics, and practices of the bodhisattva path; however, they only praise faith-understanding because [the latter] disrupts the practice.

The first verse addresses diligence (*vīrya*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*). To demonstrate that both householders and renunciants can practice the bodhisattva path, it mentions "bhikṣu" or refers to them as "bodhisattvas. Since diligence universally exerts effort and ethical discipline is the foundation of training, these two are presented at the outset.
One verse concerns giving (*dāna*) and patience (*kṣānti*); the term "equal" (*sama*) indicates that giving and patience are not one, as their types are manifold.
One verse concerns meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and one verse concerns wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “At that time, the fourfold assembly” up to “What is the cause and condition for this matter,” the commentary states:
the following one and a half verses establish the fifth [topic], the desire to hear.
The long discourse states, "Two billion bodhisattvas desire to hear the Dharma. This refers to the "fourfold assembly," as these terms mutually clarify one another.
The former [statement] is based on those who have already resolved their minds [for enlightenment], whereas these [bodhisattvas] have not yet done so.
Regarding the sūtra passage from "The Honored One venerated by gods and humans" up to "Only you can realize and know it," the commentary states:
The following four verses constitute the sixth response.

The prose section consists of four parts, while this text contains two; the first two verses explain the reasons for preaching this sutra, and the latter two verses concern the duration of the time period, omitting the brief accounts of the transmission of the lamp, the retinue, the great assembly, and the state of peace and happiness.
This is the first [point].
"Just" (適) means "near" or "beginning.

As soon as one emerges from meditative concentration, one is able to lead sentient beings to the stage of Bodhi; because this supramundane wisdom illuminates and penetrates both the ultimate and conventional truths, it is called the "Eye of the World."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "The World-Honored One praised them" up to "all are able to receive and uphold it," the commentary states:
"Time refers to the length of the period."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “The Buddha preached this Lotus Sūtra” up to “he shall enter into nirvāṇa,” the commentary states:

The preceding verse shows that the characteristics [of the past] are identical to those of the present; the following four verses eulogize the second proclamation of extinction (*parinirvāṇa*), which is distinct from the former.
This is divided into three parts:
two verses on the proclamation of his passing into extinction, one verse of admonition and exhortation for those to be converted, and one verse on the grief and distress of the great assembly.
This is the first.
When his work of transformation was finished, he proclaimed that he would now enter extinction.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, “With single-minded diligence, you may encounter [a Buddha] once in the course of a billion kalpas,” the commentary says:

This admonition exhorts those to be transformed: diligence is the root of transcendence from the world, while negligence is the foundation of birth and death; it is logically necessary to cultivate their abandonment. How much more so now that you have encountered the Buddhas, who appear only once in billions of eons—having met them, how could you fail to cultivate their abandonment?
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The appearance of the Buddhas is joy; the preaching of the True Dharma is joy; the harmony of the Saṃgha is joy; practicing together with courageous diligence is joy.
The Sūtra [also says]: "O Sons of the World-Honored One, how could the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa have come so soon?"
The commentary states:
"The great assembly is filled with sorrow and distress.
Because the world is empty and void and the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, they give rise to sorrow and distress."
Regarding the passage from “The Holy Lord, King of Dharma” to “Do not be anxious or afraid,” the commentary states:
The third section,
concerning the prophecy of future Buddhahood, consists of two parts, spanning the final two and a half verses.

The first verse exhorts one not to give rise to grief, because there is a future Buddha upon whom one may rely; it also demonstrates that although he appears to enter nirvana, he is in truth eternal, blissful, and self-mastered.
The subsequent one and a half verses explicitly clarify the bestowal of the prophecy.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sūtra passage from “This Bodhisattva Guṇakara... up to ‘he also delivers immeasurable multitudes,’” the commentary says:
This is the prophecy.
Regarding the passage in the sutra from "In this very night the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa" to "seeking the unsurpassed path," the commentary says:
The fourth section, consisting of two verses, concerns the manifestation of entry into *nirvāṇa*:
the first verse manifests the entry into *nirvāṇa*, while the latter verse shows the loss of the excellent physician and the diligent yearning for the Path.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “This Dharma Master Wondrous Light” to “extensively proclaiming the Lotus Sūtra,” the commentary states:

The preceding twenty-nine verses praise the great cause of enjoyment while the Buddha was still proclaiming [the teaching]; the following nine verses praise the remaining four causes for practicing and transforming others after his parinirvāṇa, which are divided into four parts:

The first verse summarizes the causes for the Buddhas’ turning of the wheel of Dharma; the next verse concerns the causes for firmly consolidating the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma; the following verse concerns the cause for being able to enter [the path]; and the final six verses concern the causes for recollection.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the Sūtra passage, "These eight princes... shall see countless Buddhas," the commentary says:
This is the second cause for the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma that is virtuous, firm, and solid.

According to the Hīnayāna, during three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one encounters the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin in reverse order; specifically, at the beginning of the first eon, Śākyamuni first encounters the Buddha Śākyamuni, and subsequently encounters seventy-five thousand other Buddhas.
In the beginning of the second eon, he encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin, and further met seventy-six thousand Buddhas.
In the beginning of the third eon, he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and further met seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
During the third eon, he spent one hundred kalpas cultivating the karma for the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha. He first encountered the Buddha Vipasyin (also known as Vipaśyin).

Because he stood on one foot in praise of the Buddha Tiṣya, he surpassed nine kalpas [of practice]; therefore, it is frequently stated in the sūtras that there was a Buddha Vipaśyin ninety-one kalpas ago.

If we rely on the Mahāyāna, it is by relying on the fourth stage that a bodhisattva makes offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers and only then begins to understand the meaning of the sixteen parts of *nirvāṇa*.

Although it has been traditionally assigned to the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), this is not yet definitively settled; it merely mentions "eight Ganges-sands," so why must it necessarily correspond to the tenth stage?
Paramārtha’s commentary states:

"In the first eon, one encounters Buddhas as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers; in the second eon, one meets those of six Ganges Rivers; and in the third eon, one encounters those of seven Ganges Rivers.
Therefore, although it is said here that one attains entry into the eighth stage, it further states that one shall see innumerable Buddhas.
The Sūtra says: "Having made offerings to all Buddhas, one proceeds in succession until receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
The commentary states:
This is the third cause for entering [the path], because one subsequently attains Buddhahood.
The Sūtra says: "From the final 'God among Gods' until the deliverance of immeasurable multitudes.
The commentary states:
This is the fourth [section].
Thereafter follow six verses on the recollection of causes, divided into two parts:
the first verse is the recollection of the eight sons, and the subsequent five verses are the recollection of the eight hundred disciples.
This is the first [part].
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "This Dharma Master Wondrous Light" up to "his name was called Seeking Fame," the commentary states:
The following five verses commemorate the eight hundred disciples; this section is divided into two parts.
The first two and a half verses recall the causes of defilement, while the latter two and a half verses recall the causes of purity;
this is the former.

Regarding the "Seeker of Fame" (*yaśaskāma*): they consider noble lineage to be precious and prioritize gain, benefit, and reputation. Because their studies are mostly abandoned, they are called "seekers of fame. They possess six faults, as can be understood from the text.
“Xiè” (pronounced gǔ ài) means indolence and weariness.
“Dài” (pronounced tú hǎi) also means indolence and exhaustion.
It is sometimes written as “tái,” which likewise means exhaustion, negligence, and lethargy.
The second is being greedily attached to the fame and profit already obtained; the third is further seeking fame and profit not yet attained.
"Clan" (*zú*) refers to a category.
According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), "four neighborhoods constitute a clan"; Zheng Xuan explains this as "one hundred households."
The Sūtra says: "He also performs various wholesome deeds until their number is immeasurable.
The commentary states:
There are two [aspects] to praising the causes of purity.
The first five phrases recollect the five causes of purity, while the latter five phrases recollect the two fruits of purity.
As the Sūtra states: "From the time after that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until now, it is this very body of mine."
The commentary states:
The preceding forty verses praise and point out specific matters; the following three verses praise the mutual identity of the ancient and the modern.
There are three [points]:
The first verse concerns the person, the second verse concerns the Dharma, and the final verse provides the conclusion.
This is the first [verse].
The Sūtra says: "I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara... until he was about to preach the Lotus Sūtra."
The commentary states:
This is precisely the Dharma.
It corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra from "Now the marks are as they were in the original auspicious sign" up to "Aiding in the revelation of the meaning of the true mark."
The commentary states:
This constitutes the conclusion.

By emitting light to provide awakening, all those with a karmic connection gathered; having witnessed this, the assembly conceived a profound sense of longing and reverence. This miraculous manifestation was displayed to demonstrate that the Dharma is not empty and to reveal the realization of the profound and secret [teachings]. Therefore, it is called "Emitting Light" as an auxiliary to the meaning of the True Mark (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “All you people should now know... until ‘sufficiently seeking the Buddha-way’,” the commentary states:

The preceding forty-three verses correspond to the prose section; the following two verses constitute the third major division of the text, which addresses the assembly to encourage them to understand that the Buddha is now speaking. This [third division] has two parts:

The first verse clarifies that when the Buddha preaches the Dharma rain, the sprouts of the Path grow, causing one to advance in goodness; the latter verse clarifies that when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, it causes those seeking the Path to eliminate all doubts and sever all evils.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sutra passage: "All those who seek the three vehicles... until none remain," the commentary says:
This concludes the resolution of doubts.
The following two verses describe the raining down of the great Dharma rain and the preaching of the Great Dharma.
Completed on the fourth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Hōan era, written by the monk Gakujin of Hōryū-ji Temple.
On the twenty-second day of the tenth month of the same year, the dot was moved; it was originally located at Ennyo-bō in Kōfuku-ji.
The monk Gakujin of Hōryū-ji performed this act so that the Dharma might endure for a long time, stating that "the left-hand dot may serve as a guide," and so forth.
